title: This is what Peak Performance looks like (Physical 100)
summary: A scripted review of Netflix's Korean survival show Physical: 100. NH argues it dismantles the idea that the most muscular body is the best: strategy, teamwork and mental toughness decide the quests, the most functional athlete wins rather than the most aesthetic, and its camaraderie offers positive masculine role models. He still keeps training for looks and praises fitness for its diversity.
claims: The show's opening, with sculptures of each torso, invites viewers to equate muscle mass with capability, which is a trap
In the dead-hang quest the big muscular athletes dropped first; strategy and technique matter regardless of fitness
When men faced women in contact challenges, biology decided it; even a female bodybuilder stood no chance against a male MMA fighter
The athletes' camaraderie, with losers bowing and praising winners, shows real inclusivity under the banner of fitness that Westerners could learn from
In team challenges organisation and pacing beat stacked rosters; rushing loses
Physical 100 is ultimately about mental strength: those who make it are often the ones willing to hang on longest, not the most gifted
The show is a refreshing counter to body positivity, offering masculine role models and brotherhood
In the final strength events (holding a 100 kg stone, pushing a stone up a slope) the most impressive-looking athletes were outclassed, which he says should reinforce your decision to stay natural
The winner wasn't the biggest but the most functional; training for looks was always a trade-off against performance, and he is fine with that
Fitness is better for its diversity of physiques and sports
Women should watch it as motivation to start training, aiming to be their best rather than to outperform men
